comments.text:
Great review - like all content on this channel.
To give you an idea about MSRP and real price here in the heart of Europe, Austria....
As of time of writing (4th Nov. 2020), retailer shop/tech store prices read like this (and we are not talking ebay or scalpers here, who 1,5 - 2,5x the prices mentioned below):
2080ti on average around 1400 Euro, equals to 1641 USD/ 2283 Australian dollars,
2080Super on average around 800€, equals to 937 USD/ 1305 Australian,
the actually available AIB 3070's are around 800-1000€, equals to 937-1172 USD / 1305-1631 Australian,
the non available AIB 3080's around 900-1100€, equals to 1054-1290 USD / 1468-1794 Australian,
the odd available AIB 3090's are all above 1700€, equals >2000 USD / 2773 Australian.
As a Radeon 5700XT is currently around 500 USD here - the 6000 series prices will be in that same ballpark.
So - the 3070/3080'ies are, whichever way you put it, a price/performance bargain.
And yeah - up here, we pay 50% income tax, 1,3€ (1,5 USD) for 1 litre gasoline, ....
So - stop ranting, and be happy. Hell, for 400 USD you only get a plain cheap 1 or 2 fan (yet widely&readily available) 2060 model here... ;-)

comments.text:
From what we have been shown so far these cards look really impressive and I'm super excited that AMD can finally compete at all tiers once again. It appears that these AMD cards offer more performance per dollar than nVidia's already pretty decently priced 3000 Series so again this is great. The one thing I worry about for AMD cards though is DLSS. 

I know there aren't many games using DLSS just yet but the number of titles that will use it will is only going to increase with time and these AMD cards won't come anywhere near the performance of nVidia's cards when DLSS is enabled. So we have to really hope AMD does have an answer to this technologies but personally I would have thought if they did have something they would have announced it at this event. 

So unless AMD does have a killer DLSS tech they are holding back for some reason then the choice of which card to go for comes down to which games are most important to you. Nvidia will have a massive performance per dollar advantage in any game that uses DLSS 2.0, so if any of the games are important to you then I think nVidia wins easily unless AMD hurries up and announces their version of DLSS:
- Control, 
- Death Standing, 
- CyberPunk 2077, 
- Call of Duty: Black ops – Cold War,
- Fortnite,
- F1 2020,
- Minecraft,
- Wolfenstein : Youngblood,
- Metro Exodus,
- Battlefield V,
- Shadow of the Tomb Raider,
- Final Fantasy XV,
- Anthem,
- Bright Memory,
- Mechwarrior V: Mercenaries,
- Deliver Us The Moon,
- Monster Hunter: World,
More games will be continually added, AMD needs an answer to DLSS!

This was an okay review, but I'm still not a fan of the RTX 3000 series. Nearly identical performance as the 2080ti, but limited by VRAM and only draws 30W less. Also I'm not sure how you can call the 3070 an efficient graphics card, even when you're just saying it comparatively in regards to the 2080ti and 3080. If we look at it comparatively, it draws similar power to the 980ti, a previous flagship card that wasn't known for having an efficient architecture, and the 1080 draws less power than it, the main high end card from only 2 generations ago. And we can even go as recent as Turing. The 2070, the card this is actually replacing, uses notably less power as well. You can't just compare the card to the others in its lineup, you need to look at how it stacks up historically, which is something I don't see many techtubers do anymore. You say gamers are quick to forget Nvidia's mistakes, but everyone is quick to forget Nvidia's successes that were actually good for their consumers, and jump into the "new normal" that they try to set in place every generation.

comments.text:
RIP Kevin.

Also, how'd you get it out this early? Australian/UK release times?

So just on the RT and Tensor performance of the RTX 3070...

The RTX 3070 has 46 RT cores and 184 Tensor cores. That compares to the RTX 2080 Ti with 68 RT cores and 544 Tensor cores. Given your results indicate basically identical RT and Tensor performance, it stands to reason that each RT core in the RTX 3070 is roughly 48% faster than those in the RTX 2080 Ti, and each Tensor core about 196% faster, give or take a few percent.

I think it's arguable that NVIDIA have traded the improvements made to their 2nd gen RT cores and 3rd gen Tensor cores against die space for more CUDA cores. By keeping RT and Tensor performance roughly linear with what was expected of Turing, the die size savings by having less of each were probably reinvested partly into the doubling of FP32 CUDA.

I was personally hoping to see a more drastic uplift in RT performance this generation, but it seems like that isn't going to be the case. On that front, I guess we'll just have to see how AMD's dual mode texture units perform, though my gut feeling says not to expect anything faster than what NVIDIA is offering with dedicated RT hardware.

comments.text:
To those that say "inflation": that is indeed a thing when you compare to something not very recently. But it's clearly not the only thing in recent pricing.
However, let's compare it to GTX 970. That was released in september 2014, so practically exactly 6 years ago.
Average US inflation is 2% per year (too lazy to check exactly, but I did this computations in the past using inflation calculators online).
2% every year, aka 1.02^6 amounts to 1.1261 aka 12.61% increase in 6 years.
So, $329 (MSRP of GTX 970) with extra 12.61% amounts to.... $370. It's quite far from $500 still.

Long story short, NVidia realized there's enough "whales" who will pay more than $1000 just to have the best card, no matter the price/performance ratio, so they adjusted the stack to more like $700+ high end, $300-$500 mid end and lower than $300 to be low end.

comments.text:
@choatus  While I have not verified this, usually these kinds of rumors come from an initial source. There's even times when they all come up with the same rumors independently of each other, but they came from the same person. Essentially just because it came from multiple sources doesn't mean it's more reliable. This is an understandable conclusion though.

Regarding AMD's fulfillment capabilities, this is pure speculation based on a few bits of information you have. AMD already slotted tons of capacity @ TSMC in 2019 for this year's launch with both Zen3 and RDNA2. At the time last year when I reviewed this information, I (& others) actually speculated that this seemed like a big over subscription of TSMC's wafer capacity, in the sense of "Is AMD really going to be able to use all of this capacity?" Also, the only recent 'difficult to find for sale' product is the 3300X. I'm not aware of other production issues.

Other tech tubers (Moore's Law is Dead) mentioned that AMD should be able to execute well on their fulfillment. Scott Herkelman with AMD had even made light of another twitter comment implying they should have good supply. I'm sure they are hyper aware of mining and wouldn't have likely said this to just deceive their audience. That seems like a reasonable interpretation.

In summary, the sale of XFX older generation cards is possibly true, but also possibly false (maybe 75/25 chances?). Expected mining throughput may likely not be known as AMD is separating their GPU architectures into RDNA and CDNA, with the latter presumably being likely better at mining. There's also the fact that AMD has quite a bit of reserved fab capacity @ TSMC partially due to an Nvidia misstep with TSMC and negotiations w/Samsung. Lastly, other tech tubers and even an AMD VP indicate there will not be a supply issue. Because of this, it seems very reasonable that gamers should be able to get their hands on these cards.
